article.headline: Open-Source Job Machine Scored 740 Offers, Then Got Its Creator Hired
article.lede: Santiago Fernández de Valderrama spent 16 years running a phone repair business. When he re-entered the job market as an aspiring AI executive, he found the process opaque and unscalable — so he built a system to replace it. The result is career-ops, an open-source AI pipeline that evaluated 740 job listings, generated more than 100 tailored CVs, and secured its creator a Head of Applied AI role before he published the code.
article.body:
The tool, **career-ops**, is built on top of *Claude Code* — Anthropic's agentic coding CLI — and treats the job search as an engineering problem rather than a numbers game. At its core is a seven-block evaluation rubric applied to every listing: role archetype classification, a line-by-line CV gap analysis, seniority calibration, live salary research via web-search sub-agents, a keyword-injection personalization plan, and a *STAR*-format interview story bank that accumulates across the entire pipeline. Listings score 1–5; the system recommends against applying to anything below 4.0. *ATS*-optimized PDFs are generated via *Playwright* — a browser-automation library — and a Go terminal dashboard manages the full history without leaving the command line. Fourteen skill modes cover everything from single-offer evaluation to batch processing and automated form-filling; 45-plus companies, from Anthropic and OpenAI to Salesforce (CRM) and Twilio (TWLO), are pre-configured for direct career-page scanning.

The system's central claim is that it is a filter rather than a firehose. The README's framing is deliberate: “I spent months applying to jobs the hard way. So I engineered the system I wish I had. Companies use AI to filter candidates. I just gave candidates AI to choose companies.” A hard score floor of 4.0 and an explicit refusal to auto-submit applications are the structural safeguards against the *spray-and-pray* mass-application pattern. Whether a self-policed threshold is genuinely meaningful depends on user discipline — but the architectural intent is clear.

career-ops arrives at an uncomfortable moment for hiring. Application volumes on LinkedIn have risen 45% year-over-year, and Greenhouse (a major *ATS* vendor) CEO Daniel Chait has named the dynamic the *AI doom loop*: candidates deploy AI to beat automated filters, employers tighten those filters in response, which drives candidates toward yet more automation. Greenhouse's own survey found 70% of hiring managers trust AI to make faster decisions; only 8% of job seekers describe the process as fair. The U.S. Society for Human Resource Management reports that average cost-per-hire and time-to-hire have both risen during the period of widespread generative AI adoption — evidence that neither side is winning.

*Claude Code*'s skills architecture is what makes the implementation technically interesting. Each of career-ops's 14 modes is a markdown file defining a repeatable slash-command workflow; Claude Code reads the file and executes it as an agent. A second mechanism, the headless `claude -p` flag, spawns parallel sub-agent workers for batch evaluation. The user's CV, scoring preferences, and career archetypes live in a persistent `CLAUDE.md` context file that every agent inherits automatically — eliminating re-prompting on each run and giving the system a coherent memory of the candidate across all 740 evaluations.

Commercial auto-apply services — Sonara, LazyApply, Loopcv — compete on volume, submitting hundreds of applications with minimal user review. career-ops inverts that logic: the automation is in the evaluation, not the submission. The creator's own résumé is the only peer-reviewed evidence the system works at scale, and recruiters' concerns about AI-inflated application volumes apply here too, even if less directly. The tool's 43,000 GitHub stars in under a week suggest that the demand it is capturing is not laziness so much as exhaustion — a felt need to impose order on a hiring market that, for many candidates, seems to have none.

concepts.definition: Software used by employers to collect, filter, and rank job applications before a human recruiter reviews them. The system parses resumes for keywords drawn from the job description, then scores or eliminates candidates automatically. Most large employers use ATS, which means a resume may never reach a human if it lacks the right keywords or uses incompatible formatting.

Anthropic's agentic coding CLI tool that reads codebases, edits files, runs shell commands, and executes multi-step workflows. It supports a “skills” architecture in which repeatable tasks are defined as markdown slash-command files that the agent reads and runs. career-ops is implemented entirely as a collection of these skills.

The job-search strategy of submitting as many applications as possible with minimal tailoring, betting that volume compensates for a low individual match rate. Automated tools such as LazyApply and Sonara are built around this approach. career-ops explicitly positions itself as the structural opposite.

A structured storytelling framework used in job interviews: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Candidates prepare short anecdotes in this format to answer behavioral questions. career-ops builds a running story bank in STAR format that is enriched with each new job evaluation, accumulating reusable interview material across the whole search.

A term coined by Greenhouse CEO Daniel Chait to describe a self-reinforcing cycle in hiring: job seekers use AI to submit more applications to beat ATS filters, which increases application volume, which leads employers to tighten their filters, which pushes candidates toward even more automation. Both sides emerge worse off.

An open-source browser-automation library, originally developed at Microsoft, that controls web browsers programmatically via code. career-ops uses it both to scrape company career pages for job listings and to render HTML CV templates to PDF through a browser engine — ensuring consistent, professionally formatted output.

repos.summary: An MIT-licensed, AI-powered job search pipeline built on Claude Code. It evaluates job listings through a seven-block scoring rubric, generates keyword-tailored PDFs, and manages the full application lifecycle through a Go terminal dashboard built with Bubble Tea and Lipgloss. The creator used it to evaluate 740 listings and land a Head of Applied AI role before open-sourcing the code; the repository accumulated 43,000 stars within a week of publication.

article.fact_check: Widely shared secondary tweets — notably from @heygurisingh and @alex_prompter — describe the creator as having been “laid off” before building career-ops. The creator's own README and published case study make no such claim: they describe him as having sold a phone repair business and then entered the job market as a career changer pursuing AI roles. The “laid off” framing appears to be narrative embellishment added by amplifiers to make the story more sympathetic, and is not a detail the original poster or creator has confirmed.

ticker_crm.name: Salesforce, Inc.
ticker_crm.blurb: Salesforce is a leading cloud-based software company specializing in customer relationship management (CRM) solutions. It offers a suite of enterprise applications for sales, service, marketing, analytics, and artificial intelligence. The company has been pivoting to position itself as an AI agent company, integrating generative AI into its platform. Salesforce is a major player in the enterprise software market, competing with the likes of Microsoft and Oracle.
ticker_crm.recent: In the past 30 days, CRM stock jumped as Salesforce emphasized its transformation into an AI agent company, highlighting new AI-powered features. The company's focus on AI has been a key catalyst for recent price action, with investors reacting positively to its strategic direction. No major earnings reports were released in this period.

ticker_twlo.blurb: Twilio Inc. provides a customer engagement platform that enables developers to build communications and customer interactions into applications via APIs. Its offerings include messaging, voice, email, video, and identity solutions, as well as the Segment customer data platform. The company serves businesses globally and is a leader in the cloud communications platform-as-a-service market.
